claim: Indus legends are built from seven word classes: numerals, links, the names of great households, personal-name elements, commodities and units, office nouns and closing determinatives. A seal legend reads "of [household]: [personal name], [department] [office] [the man or the body]". The pair of short strokes after the openers 817, 861 and 820 is a particle meaning "of"; the fish signs are "star" elements of personal names; the jar 740 is the steward of the store named by the sign before it; the comb 400 marks an office as a body and the man 090 an individual holder. Harappa's moulded and incised tablets are tokens of standard measures, offices and labour; Mohenjo-daro's copper tablets record named holders and their fodder or grain allotments; pottery marks give capacities in standard units or the store a vessel belongs to. Because names and commodities belong to a city while households, offices and grammar are shared, and because office holders have larger seals bearing the emblem of the shared administration, the classes predict where seals were found, their size, their animal and their date. The full map is GLOSS-MAP.json and the reading READING.md.

claim: The animal on an Indus seal marks the holder's affiliation, and the unicorn affiliation was a single body present in every city. Rarer animals mark smaller affiliations, each based in fewer places. The affiliation is shown by the animal and is not written in the legend, so holders of the same title in different affiliations carry the same text with different animals.

claim: Harappa's moulded and incised tablets are standard tokens issued in series. One face names what the token is for, and the face with two, three or four tall strokes before sign 700 states its tier: two, three or four of a standard unit. On seals, by contrast, stroke groups are fixed parts of names and titles, and do not count goods.
